chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ahmad ibn Ishaq from Yasir the servant who said:

Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) passed by me while I was praying on the tabariyy (prayer stone), and I had placed something on it upon which I prostrate. He said to me, 'What is wrong with you that you do not prostrate on it? Is it not from the vegetation of the earth?' This report is attributed to the state of taqiyya (dissimulation).
Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from Ali ibn Mahziyar who said:

Dawud ibn Yazid asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about the qaratis and kawaghiz (paper sheets) written upon them, whether it is permissible to prostrate on them or not, so he wrote, 'It is permissible.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: There is no contradiction between this report and the report of Jamil ibn Darraj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), because that report is attributed to karahah (dislike/preference) and is explicit in it, and there is nothing in it from the words of prohibition (hazr).

key_terms.اَلتَّقِيَّة: Dissimulation or precautionary concealment of belief
key_terms.اَلطَّبَرِيِّ: A type of prayer stone or surface

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to prostrate on paper during Islamic prayer according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This passage from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the permissibility of prostrating on written paper (qaratis/kawaghiz) by reconciling two reports through the lens of *taqiyya* (dissimulation) and *karahah* (dislike). While one report attributes the Imam’s question about not prostrating on a plant-based surface to *taqiyya*, the explicit permission granted to Dawud ibn Yazid confirms that writing does not invalidate the prostration surface, provided it is not treated with excessive reverence. This distinction highlights the Shia scholarly approach to resolving apparent contradictions by differentiating between mere dislike and strict prohibition.
